If we look at the `longitude` and `latitude` values for the city at index 157 (labeled 96), they look pretty close to those of city 0. So, in this case, the closest city to city 0 is city 157 and the Euclidean distance between the two cities is 0.184. ::: --- ## Finding the distances to a query point ::: {#e5fc41a4 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} query_point = [[-80, 25]] dists = euclidean_distances(train_df[["longitude", "latitude"]], query_point) dists[0:5] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` array([[19.54996348], [18.02706204], [24.60912622], [21.39718237], [25.24111312]]) ``` ::: :::
We can find the city closest to the query point (-80, 25) using: ::: {#2a9d6d18 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} np.argmin(dists) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` np.int64(147) ``` ::: :::
The distance between the query point and closest city is: ::: {#ddb479ae .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} dists[np.argmin(dists)].item() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` 3.8383922936564634 ``` ::: ::: :::{.notes} Next, let’s find the distances to a given query point. Before we were calculating the distances between all the cities in our training dataset to all other cities in the same set. But what if instead, we are given this new query point which does not occur in our training data. So, suppose we have the query point with a longitude value of -80 and a latitude value of 25. We want to find the training example that's most similar to this query point. How can we do that? First, we calculate the distances from a credit point to all examples in our training set. We are showing the distances of our query point to the first five cities in our training data. Next, we find out which city from our training data the query point is closest to. It turns out that the city at index 147 is close to our point with the Euclidean distance between the two equal to 3.838. ::: --- ::: {#4967da82 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1) nn.fit(train_df[['longitude', 'latitude']]); nn.kneighbors([[-80, 25]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` (array([[3.83839229]]), array([[147]])) ``` ::: ::: :::{.notes} We use Sklearn's `NearestNeighbors` function to get the closest example and the distance between the query point and the closest example. First, we create our “class” object (we can specify the number of closest neighbours we wish to find), we train on it, and then we can pass our query example to our object to return the closest number of examples along with the distances. And we could also extend it to points in multi-dimensional space. All this matches our intuition of "distance" in the real world. ::: --- ::: {#49fb99c3 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} pokemon_df = pd.read_csv("data/pokemon.csv") X = pokemon_df.drop(columns = ['deck_no', 'name','total_bs', 'type', 'legendary']) y = pokemon_df[['legendary']] X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=123) X_train.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ```{=html}
